Unmerciful Servant
un-MUR-sih-ful SUR-vant
noun phrase (Matthew 18)
From the parable of Matthew 18; the servant forgiven a vast debt who refused to forgive his fellow a small one, and was delivered to the tormentors.

Biblical Definition

The unmerciful servant is the figure of our Lord's parable in Matthew 18, told in answer to Peter's question how often he must forgive his brother. A king took account of his servants and found one owing ten thousand talents—an unpayable sum, the wages of many lifetimes—and when the servant could not pay and begged for patience, the king was moved with compassion, loosed him, and forgave him the whole debt. But that same servant went out, found a fellow-servant owing him a hundred pence—a trifling sum—took him by the throat, and cast him into prison till he should pay. When his lord heard of it, he called him: “O thou wicked servant, I forgave thee all that debt, because thou desiredst me: shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?” And he delivered him to the tormentors till he should pay all. The Lord drives the lesson home: “So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses.” The dictionary holds the parable to teach that the believer, forgiven an infinite debt by God, is bound to forgive the comparatively trifling wrongs done to him. The unforgiving spirit is not a small fault but the mark of one who has not understood or received the grace he professes; an unforgiven heart toward others betrays a heart that has never truly known forgiveness from God. The dictionary marks the parable against the cheap grace that severs forgiveness from a forgiving life, and against the works-righteousness that would make our forgiving the ground of God's; rather, God's vast mercy is the ground and motive of ours, and the absence of mercy toward others exposes the absence of grace within.

Webster 1828 Definition

The servant of Christ's parable forgiven an unpayable debt who refused his fellow a trifling one, and was delivered to the tormentors (Matthew 18:32-35); the forgiven who will not forgive betrays a heart that has not received grace.

UNMERCIFUL SERVANT, noun phrase. The servant of Matthew 18 forgiven a vast debt who would not forgive a small one.

Told in answer to Peter's question how often he must forgive (Matthew 18:21).

Forgiven ten thousand talents, he jailed a fellow owing a hundred pence.

“Shouldest not thou also have had compassion… even as I had pity on thee?” (Matthew 18:33).

“So likewise shall my heavenly Father do… if ye from your hearts forgive not” (Matthew 18:35).

Key Scripture

Mt 18:32 — "Then his lord, after that he had called him, said unto him, O thou wicked servant, I forgave thee all that debt, because thou desiredst me:"

Mt 18:33 — "Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?"

Mt 18:35 — "So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses."

Mt 18:21 — "Then came Peter to him, and said, Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?"

Modern Corruption

Cheap grace severs forgiveness from a forgiving life, while works-righteousness makes our forgiving the ground of God's; both miss that God's vast mercy is the ground and motive of ours.

expand to see more

Cheap grace hears the parable's comfort—the unpayable debt forgiven—and ignores its warning, severing God's forgiveness from any forgiving life in the one forgiven. But the Lord makes the unforgiving servant a wicked servant, delivered to the tormentors, and applies it directly: so shall the Father do to those who will not forgive their brethren from the heart. The dictionary names the error: a professed faith that leaves the heart hard and vengeful toward others is exposed by this parable as a faith that has never truly received the grace it claims. The forgiven forgive; the unforgiving show they were never forgiven.

The opposite error reads the parable as works-righteousness, as though our forgiving others earned or caused God's forgiveness of us. The order of the parable forbids this: the king forgave the great debt first, freely, moved with compassion, before any question of the servant's mercy arose. God's prior, vast, unmerited mercy is the ground and the motive of ours; we forgive because we have been forgiven, not in order to be. The dictionary holds the balance: forgiveness is received by grace, not earned by forgiving; and the grace truly received unfailingly produces a forgiving heart, so that the refusal to forgive is the surest sign that grace has not been received at all.

Hebrew Roots

From the parable's contrast of debts: ten thousand “talents” (a vast sum) against a hundred “pence” (Greek denaria, a trifle); the “tormentors” (Greek basanistes) figure the judgment on the unforgiving.

expand to see more

Talanton, Greek, a talent, an enormous sum; ten thousand was beyond all payment.

Denarion, Greek, a penny, a day's wage; a hundred was a trifling debt.

Basanistes, Greek, a tormentor or jailer, to whom the wicked servant was delivered.

“From your hearts” (Greek apo ton kardion) marks true forgiveness as inward, not formal.

Peter's “till seven times” is answered by “until seventy times seven” (Matthew 18:22).

Usage

"The pastor preached the unmerciful servant to show that the forgiven must forgive, or prove they were never forgiven."

"He warned that an unforgiving heart is no small fault but the mark of grace unreceived."

"She forgave the wrong done her, remembering the vast debt her Lord had freely cancelled."
